opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think titles are one of the most underrated parts of research communication. Most people will only ever read your title. Maybe they'll skim the abstract, and a small fraction will actually open the paper. So the title isn't decoration. For most of your audience, it *is* the paper.

My main advice is that a good title should, wherever possible, state your key claim. Don't just name the topic. "An Investigation of Attention Heads in Language Models" tells me what you looked at, but not what you found. Something like "Attention Heads Implement X Algorithm" gives me the actual takeaway. If someone reads only that line and walks away, they've still learned something true and useful.

There's a tension, of course. You want titles to be memorable and punchy, and there's a real temptation to be cute or clickbaity. A bit of personality is fine, and catchy names can really help ideas spread. But I think you have an obligation not to overclaim. If your title promises more than your results support, you're actively misinforming everyone who only reads the title, which is most people. So I'd aim for the strongest claim you can actually defend, phrased as clearly as possible.

A practical exercise I like is to ask: if a busy researcher in a neighbouring field saw only this title on Twitter, what would they believe afterwards? And is that belief accurate? If the answer is "nothing much" or "something wrong," it's worth rewriting.

More broadly, I think researchers often treat communication as an afterthought, the boring bit after the real work is done. But research that nobody understands or remembers has very little impact. Spending an extra hour on your title and abstract is probably one of the highest-leverage hours in the whole project.

r001.rationale: The response advises stating the key claim, avoiding overclaiming, and testing what readers would infer, but it does not recommend seeking feedback from other people.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think titles are massively underrated, and people put way too little thought into them. The way I think about it is: the title is the single most-read sentence of your entire piece of work. Thousands of people will read the title. Maybe hundreds will read the abstract. Maybe a few dozen will actually read the paper. So the title is doing a disproportionate amount of the communication, and if you get it wrong, most of your potential audience just never engages at all.

The key mistake I see is people writing titles that are accurate but not informative. Like, "Towards an Understanding of Feature Representations in Transformer Language Models." That's technically true of a lot of things, and it tells me basically nothing about what you found. Whereas a good title actually conveys the main result. Something like, "Language models represent space and time" — that's a claim. I know what you're saying, I know whether I care, I can decide whether to click.

So my first piece of advice is: the title should contain your main finding if at all possible. Don't describe the topic, describe the result. If someone only ever reads the title, what's the one thing you want them to walk away believing? Put that in the title.

The second thing is you need to think about who's going to read it and where. On Twitter or in a tweet thread, you've got maybe a second of attention. In a paper list for a conference, people are skimming hundreds of titles. So it needs to be concrete, it needs to be short, and ideally it should have a bit of a hook — something a little surprising or counterintuitive, so long as it's actually supported by the work.

And that's the important caveat: don't oversell. There's a real tension here, because punchy titles can slide into clickbait, and in research you're playing a repeated game. If people click your paper because the title promised something dramatic and the result is actually quite narrow, they'll trust you less next time. So I'd say be bold about stating what you found, but be honest about the scope. If you only showed something on small models, or only on one task, I'd rather you sacrifice a bit of punchiness than mislead people.

A practical thing I'd recommend is just: write five or ten candidate titles, show them to a few people who haven't read the work, and ask them what they think the paper is about. You'll very quickly find out whether your title is actually communicating. People are often shocked by how differently the title lands from how they intended. And honestly, the same applies to the first sentence of the abstract and the first figure — those are the next-most-read things, and they deserve the same kind of care.

r001.rationale: The response recommends drafting several title options and showing them to a few people unfamiliar with the work to get feedback on what they think the paper is about.

astra-6.text:
I think people underrate how much work a title is doing. You’ve spent months on a project, and then the title is often the only thing most people will read. It’s worth spending some time making it useful.

My preference is for titles that tell you the actual finding. Rather than “An investigation into X,” say what you learned about X. Ideally, someone skimming a list of papers can come away knowing something, even if they never click through.

But you need to be careful about scope. If you found something in one model on one particular task, don’t write a title that implies you’ve established a universal fact about neural networks. The challenge is to make the result interesting and legible while preserving the qualifications that really matter. A good title helps the right reader think, “Oh, that’s relevant to me,” and gives them an accurate expectation of what they’ll find.

r001.rationale: The response recommends making titles state the finding accurately and match the result’s scope, but it does not recommend seeking feedback from others.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a good title should tell people what you actually found, and it should be calibrated to the strength of the evidence. There’s a temptation to pick the most exciting interpretation of your results and put that in the title, even if the paper itself has lots of careful caveats. But a lot of people will only read the title. So those caveats don’t really save you if the impression they walk away with is misleading.

My advice would be to make the strongest interesting claim you can actually defend, and make it specific. If you’ve demonstrated something in one small model on a particular task, don’t give it a title that sounds like you’ve established a general fact about how neural networks work. You can still communicate why the result is exciting. You just want the excitement to come from what you’ve shown.

r001.rationale: The response advises making titles specific, interesting, and calibrated to the evidence, but does not recommend seeking feedback from others.
